title: Koga Miyata Bicycle Computer
description: Designed a bicycle-mounted computer for Koga Miyata combining turn-by-turn navigation with location-aware tourist information, purpose-built for touring cyclists through dedicated user research.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: Koga Miyata (Dutch bicycle manufacturer), early-career project completed in 2000 as part of an Industrial Design Engineering degree at TU Delft. This is included as an example of early product thinking, not as a product management case study.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: The bicycle computer market served road racers and commuters. Touring cyclists — who travel long distances through unfamiliar territory and are interested in their environment — had no product built for their specific needs. Koga Miyata wanted a brand extension that served this segment and matched their premium positioning.

sections.title: My role
sections.body: I owned the full project scope: market research, user research, concept definition, and interaction design. This was an individual academic project with a real client brief.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: Research focused on the touring cyclist segment specifically: routes, information needs on the road, and how they solved navigation at the time. I analysed competing products, interviewed touring cyclists, and reviewed adjacent categories including early GPS devices and PDAs. The product concept combined turn-by-turn navigation with location-aware tourist information — addressing the segment's actual context rather than adapting a commuter product.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: A complete product concept covering information architecture, interaction model, and physical form factor. The tourist information layer was positioned as a natural extension of navigation rather than a separate feature. The project established a discipline of segment-specific research before product definition that has informed my approach throughout my career.
